## Introduction

### Overview & learning goals

One of R's most powerful features is its
**built-in ability to deal with tabular data** ---
i.e., data with rows and columns like those familiar from Excel
spreadsheets and so on.
R stores tabular data in a data structure called a "**data frame**".

In this lecture, you will learn:

- The vector data structure, R's main data types, and comparisons
- Data frames and different functions to reorganize and modify data frames
- How to look at data frames in Positron's Data Explorer
- How to read and write files with tabular data

### Setting up

1. Open Positron and connect to OSC with your personal dir open,
   like in the [previous lecture](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#setup-starting-positron-and-connecting-to-osc).
2. Create a new folder `week13` in your personal dir,
   and [open it in Positron](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#working-directory-and-opening-a-folder).
3. Create a new Quarto document `week13a.qmd` in it, and add a YAML header.

## Vectors and data types

Before turning to tabular data, you'll learn about two of R's nuts and bolts:

- **Data structures** are the kinds of objects that R can store data in:
  - Here, you'll learn about the simplest one, the **vector**.
  - Later in this lecture, you'll learn about the data structure for tabular data: the _data frame_.
- **Data types** are how R distinguishes between different kinds of data,
  like numbers versus character strings.

### Vectors

A vector in R is a collection of one or more items,
which we'll call **elements**.
A common way to make a vector is with the `c()` (combine) function ---
for example, to store the number of RNA-seq reads for three genes:

```{r}
read_counts <- c(500, 1200, 300)
read_counts
```

A single value, like `500`, is also a vector, with one element.

Next, let's store the IDs of these genes:

```{r}
gene_ids <- c("geneA", "geneB", "geneC")
gene_ids
```

These IDs are **character strings** (_strings_ for short):

- Each string, like `"geneA"`, constitutes **one** element,
  not 5 (its number of characters).
- Unlike numbers, strings have to be **quoted**^[
  Either double quotes (`"..."`) or single quotes (`'...'`) work,
  but the former are more commonly used.].
  This doesn't mean the quotes are part of the string itself:
  they are just a way to tell R that it is a string.

Recall that anything that is not quoted is interpreted as an object,
like `iris` in the previous lecture.
Therefore, the code below doesn't work, because there is no _object_ called `geneA`:

```{r, error=TRUE}
c(geneA, geneB, geneC)
```

To make a vector with a **series of whole numbers**, you can use the `:` operator:

```{r}
1:10
```

### Vectorization

Consider the output of this command:

```{r}
read_counts / 1000
```

Above, **every individual element in `read_counts` was divided by 1000**.
This behavior,
where an operation is automatically applied to every element of a vector,
is called "vectorization" --- a key feature of the R language.

Many functions are vectorized too,
like `log2()`, which you can use to log-transform counts:

```{r}
log2(read_counts)
```

Other functions instead _summarize_ a vector,
like `length()` to get the number of elements,
and `mean()` to compute the mean:

```{r}
length(read_counts)
mean(read_counts)
```

For more functions like these, see the [optional R self-study page](../bonus/r.qmd#exploring-vectors).

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 1: Vectorization

Longer genes get more reads simply because they are longer,
so a common step in RNA-seq analysis is to divide read counts by gene length.
Start by creating a vector with the lengths (in kilobases)
of the three genes in `read_counts`:

```{r}
gene_lengths_kb <- c(2, 4, 1.5)
```

1. What do you think the following code will return?
   We didn't cover this kind of scenario, but go ahead and test your intuition!

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   read_counts / gene_lengths_kb
   ```

   a) `250 300 200`
   b) `266.6667` (a single number)
   c) Nine numbers: each count divided by each gene length
   d) An error, because you can't divide a vector by another vector

   After you've decided, run the code and check if you were correct.

   <!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   **a)** is correct:

   ```{r}
   read_counts / gene_lengths_kb
   ```

   Both vectors have 3 elements, which leads to "element-wise matching":
   the first element of the first vector is divided by the first element of the second vector,
   the second element by the second element, and so on.

   </details>
   ---->

2. Now say that you have gene lengths in base pairs instead:

   ```{r}
   gene_lengths_bp <- c(2000, 4000, 1500)
   ```

   Which of these computes the number of reads per kilobase for each gene,
   giving the same result as above?

   a) `read_counts / gene_lengths_bp`
   b) `read_counts / gene_lengths_bp / 1000`
   c) `read_counts / (gene_lengths_bp / 1000)`

   After you've decided, run all three lines and check if you were correct.

   <!----
   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   **c)** is correct:

   ```{r}
   read_counts / (gene_lengths_bp / 1000)
   ```

   Option a) computes the number of reads per base pair instead.

   Option c) combines both kinds of vectorization:
   `gene_lengths_bp / 1000` divides each length by the single number 1000,
   and the counts are then divided element-wise by the resulting lengths.

   The parentheses matter: option b) is calculated from left to right,
   so it divides by 1000 instead of multiplying by it.
   (`read_counts / gene_lengths_bp * 1000` does work.)

   </details>
   ---->
:::

### Extracting elements from vectors

Extracting elements from objects like vectors is often called **"indexing"**.
In R, you can do this with square brackets `[ ]`.

- Get the second element with `[2]`^[
  R starts counting at 1 like humans do, so index 2 is simply the second element.
  Python and several other languages instead start counting at 0.]:

  ```{r}
  gene_ids[2]
  ```

- Get the first and third elements with `[c(1, 3)]`:

  ```{r}
  read_counts[c(1, 3)]
  ```

In other words, you extract elements from a vector by using _another vector_,
whose values are the positions of the elements in the original vector.

### Data types

R distinguishes between different kinds of data, such as character strings and numbers,
using several pre-defined "data types".
R's behavior depends heavily on the data type.
For example, R refuses to perform mathematical operations on character strings,
so the code below returns an error:

```{r, error=TRUE}
gene_ids * 2
```

You can ask what type of data something is with the `typeof()` function:

```{r}
typeof(gene_ids)
typeof(read_counts)
```

R set the data type of `gene_ids` to `character`, i.e. (character) strings,
and that of `read_counts` to `double`, i.e. numbers.
**Anything** that is placed between quotes is a `character` --- even plain numbers:

```{r}
typeof("300")
```

Besides `character`, there are three other **common data types**.
Here is an overview,
including the abbreviations you'll often see in R output:

| Data type            | Abbreviation  | Explanation                          | Example          |
|----------------------|---------------|--------------------------------------|------------------|
| `double` / `numeric` | `dbl` / `num` | Numbers that can have decimal points | `3.14`           |
| `integer`            | `int`         | Whole numbers                        | `1:3`            |
| `character`          | `chr`         | Character strings                    | `"geneA"`, `"5"` |
| `logical`            | `lgl`         | `TRUE` or `FALSE` (unquoted!)        | `TRUE`           |

: {.striped .hover}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
### Whole numbers you type yourself are still stored as doubles _(Click to expand)_

For example:

```{r}
typeof(5)
```

While numbers are stored as integers when you create them with `:`:

```{r}
typeof(1:3)
```

To force R to store a number as an integer, you can add an `L` after it:

```{r}
typeof(5L)
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
:::

### Comparing things

R returns `logical`s when you **compare** things.
Comparisons are vectorized too,
so you get a `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each element ---
for example, to check which genes have more than 400 reads:

```{r}
read_counts > 400
```

To test whether things are equal,
don't forget to use **two** equals signs `==`:

```{r}
gene_ids == "geneB"
```

Logicals can be used as if they were numbers,
where `TRUE` represents 1 and `FALSE` represents 0.
This provides an easy way to _count_ how many elements meet a condition,
like the number of genes with more than 400 reads:

```{r}
sum(read_counts > 400)
```

You'll use this in week 15, for example to count the number of genes
that are significantly differentially expressed.

Here are the most common comparison operators in R:

| **Operator** | **Description**          | **Example**              |
|--------------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| `>`          | Greater than             | 5 \> 6 returns `FALSE`   |
| `<`          | Less than                | 5 \< 6 returns `TRUE`    |
| `==`         | Equal to                 | 10 == 10 returns `TRUE`  |
| `!=`         | Not equal to             | 10 != 10 returns `FALSE` |
| `>=`         | Greater than or equal to | 5 \>= 6 returns `FALSE`  |
| `<=`         | Less than or equal to    | 6 \<= 6 returns `TRUE`   |

: {.striped .hover}

### A vector can only contain one data type

A vector can only be composed of **a single data type**.
So when you combine different data types into one vector,
R silently converts them all to the same type ---
for example, numbers to strings:

```{r}
c(500, 1200, "300")
```

This **type coercion** can be the source of surprises:
for example, if a single value in a column of numbers in a file is not a number,
R will read the whole column as `character`.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: Data types

For each line of code below, what do you think the data type (if any) will be?
Try it out and see if you were right.

1. `typeof("TRUE")`

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   `"TRUE"` is `character` (and not `logical`) because of the quotes around it:

   ```{r}
   typeof("TRUE")
   ```

   </details>

2. `typeof(geneA)`

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   This returns an error because the object `geneA` does not exist.
   Any unquoted string (that is not a special keyword like `TRUE` and `FALSE`)
   is interpreted as a reference to an object.

   ```{r, error=TRUE}
   typeof(geneA)
   ```

   </details>

3. `typeof(c(1.5, TRUE, FALSE))`

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   This produces a `double` vector:
   the logicals are coerced to numbers, with `TRUE` becoming 1 and `FALSE` becoming 0.

   ```{r}
   c(1.5, TRUE, FALSE)
   typeof(c(1.5, TRUE, FALSE))
   ```

   </details>
:::

### Missing values (`NA`)

R uses `NA` to represent **missing data**,
which is important in statistical computing,
as not all measurements are always available.
For example, in week 15, you'll see that some genes get `NA` as their p-value.
`NA` is not a character string, so it is not quoted
(just like `TRUE` and `FALSE`):

```{r}
pvals <- c(0.001, NA, 0.2, 0.04)
pvals
```

Many functions that operate on vectors will return `NA` if **any** element is `NA`,
so you can't directly count the number of p-values below 0.05:

```{r}
sum(pvals < 0.05)
```

You can get around this by setting `na.rm = TRUE` ("remove `NA`s") in such functions:

```{r}
sum(pvals < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

To check which elements are `NA`, use the `is.na()` function:

```{r}
is.na(pvals)
```

## Data frames

Data frames are another R data structure,
which can be thought of as vectors pasted side-by-side:
each column is a vector, and can therefore only contain one data type.
This also means that rows and columns aren't equivalent:
each column is a variable, and each row an observation.

For example, you can combine the gene vectors from above into a data frame
with the `data.frame()` function,
where each argument creates a column (`<column-name> = <vector>`):

```{r}
gene_df <- data.frame(
  gene_id = gene_ids,
  count = read_counts,
  length_kb = gene_lengths_kb
)
gene_df
```

Each row is now a gene, and each column a variable,
with a `character` vector in the first column and `double`s in the other two.

### The penguins data set

To explore data frames, and to visualize data in the next lecture,
we'll use the `penguins` data set, which comes with R.
It contains measurements on 3 species of penguins collected on 3 islands in Antarctica.
It has 344 observations (rows) and 8 variables (columns):

- `species`: Species of penguin (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo)
- `island`: Island where the penguin was found (Biscoe, Dream, Torgersen)
- `bill_len`: Length of the penguin's bill in millimeters
- `bill_dep`: Depth of the penguin's bill in millimeters
- `flipper_len`: Length of the penguin's flipper in millimeters
- `body_mass`: Body mass of the penguin in grams
- `sex`: Sex of the penguin
- `year`: Year of data collection

Because `penguins` has 344 rows, let's use `head()` to print only its first few rows:

```{r}
head(penguins)
```

### Looking at a data frame in the Data Explorer

To look at a data frame in a spreadsheet-like view,
run the `View()` function to open it in Positron's **Data Explorer**.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
View(penguins)
# (Should open the data frame in a new editor tab)
```

The Data Explorer also includes a **summary panel** that shows, for each column,
its data type, the percentage of missing values, and a small plot of its distribution.

<!---- TODO: Add a screenshot of penguins in the Data Explorer ---->

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
For data frames that are listed in the Variables pane (any that you create yourself),
you can also click the table icon next to them.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Sorting and filtering in the Data Explorer _(Click to expand)_

You can also sort and filter rows in the Data Explorer,
similar to the `arrange()` and `filter()` functions that you'll learn about below:

- To **sort**, click the three dots in a column header,
  and select `Sort Ascending` or `Sort Descending`.
- To **filter**, click `+ Add Filter` in the filter bar at the top,
  pick a column, and choose a condition.
  You can add multiple filters.

Like Filter functionality in Excel, this only changes what you _see_:
the data frame itself is not modified.
Steps that are part of your analysis should be in your code,
so that they are reproducible.
Here, the Data Explorer can help: after sorting and/or filtering,
click the **Convert to Code** button to get the R code that
does the same sorting and filtering, which you can copy into your document.
:::

### Working with data frames

To get only a data frame's dimensions, use `nrow()` for the number of rows,
`ncol()` for the number of columns, or `dim()` for both:

```{r}
dim(penguins)
```

You can extract individual columns from a data frame using the `$` operator.
This returns a vector, so we'll use `head()` again to show only its first elements:

```{r}
head(penguins$body_mass)
```

Like any vector, it can be indexed with `[ ]`:

```{r}
penguins$body_mass[2]
```

## The tidyverse

We'll start working with a family of R packages designed for "dataframe-centric"
data science called the ["tidyverse"](https://www.tidyverse.org).
Dataframe-centric refers to doing most if not all data analysis while keeping
the data in R's data frame data structure.

All core tidyverse packages can be installed and loaded with a single command.
You installed the tidyverse
[at the end of last week's lecture](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#before-next-week-install-packages-for-week-13),
so you only need to **load** it now:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

The output tells you which packages have been loaded as part of the tidyverse.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
### Why you get a warning about "Conflicts"  _(Click to expand)_

When you loaded the tidyverse,
the output included a  "Conflicts" section that may have seemed ominous:

```r-out-solo
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
```

What this means is that two tidyverse functions, `filter()` and `lag()`,
have the same names as two functions from the _stats_ package that were already
in your R environment.

Those stats package functions are part of what is often referred to as "base R":
core R functionality that is always available (loaded) when you start R.

Due to this function name conflict/collision,
the `filter()` function from _dplyr_ "masks" the `filter()` function from _stats_.
Therefore, if you write a command with `filter()`,
it will use the _dplyr_ function and not the _stats_ function.

You _can_ use a "masked" function,
by prefacing it with its package name as follows: `stats::filter()`.
:::

### Tidy data

The tidyverse is named after the concept of "tidy data" [@wickham2014],
a way of organizing tabular data that follows three rules:

1. Each variable is a column.
2. Each observation is a row.
3. Each value is a cell.

For example, the following table with plant height measurements is **not** tidy,
because the time point variable is spread across two column names:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}


| plant | height_7dpi | height_14dpi |
| ----- | ----------- | ------------ |
| P1    | 10.2        | 15.1         |
| P2    | 9.8         | 14.3         |

:::
::: {.column width="25%"}

:::
:::


<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Here is the same data in **tidy form**,
with separate columns for the time point and the height:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

| plant | dpi | height |
| ----- | --- | ------ |
| P1    | 7   | 10.2   |
| P1    | 14  | 15.1   |
| P2    | 7   | 9.8    |
| P2    | 14  | 14.3   |

:::
::: {.column width="25%"}

:::
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The `penguins` data set is an example of tidy data, with one row for each penguin.

::: callout-tip
#### Organizing your spreadsheet data

Tidyverse functions are designed to work with tidy data,
so organizing your data this way from the start
will make your analyses easier.
That said, a wide format can be more convenient for entering data,
for example when you add a column after each measurement round.
That is fine, since you can reshape data in R with
`pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`,
as you'll see in [Wednesday's lecture](w13b_data-viz.qmd#reshaping-data-for-plotting).
:::

### Tibbles

The tidyverse has its own variant of a data frame, called a **tibble**.
The main difference is the nicer default printing behavior of tibbles:
e.g. the data types of columns are shown,
and only a limited number of rows are printed.

To turn a regular data frame into a tibble, use the `as_tibble()` function.
Let's do that for `penguins`, and assign the result back to the same name:

```{r}
penguins <- as_tibble(penguins)
penguins
```

The `fct` in the output stands for **factor**, a data type for categorical data
(more on factors [below](#setting-a-custom-order-with-factors)).

## Subsetting and sorting with _dplyr_

The _dplyr_ package provides useful functions for
**manipulating data in data frames**, such as for "data wrangling":
cleaning and transforming your data to make it easier to visualize and analyze.
In this lecture, we'll cover some of the most commonly used _dplyr_ functions:

- `select()` to pick columns (variables)
- `filter()` to pick rows (observations)
- `arrange()` to change the order of rows (i.e., to sort a data frame)
- `mutate()` to modify values in columns and create new columns
- `summarize()` to compute across-row summaries

All these functions have the same input/output behavior:

- Their input is a data frame
- Their output is a **new, modified** data frame

### `select()` to pick columns (variables)

The first `dplyr` function you'll learn about is `select()`,
which subsets a data frame by including/excluding certain columns.
By default, it only **includes the columns you specify**:

```{r}
select(.data = penguins, body_mass, species, island)
```

Above, the first argument was the data frame,
whereas the other arguments were the names of columns to be included
in the output data frame.
Note that each column is a separate argument:
you don't combine the column names into a vector with `c()`.
Other _dplyr_ functions that take multiple columns work the same way.

::: callout-tip
#### Why aren't the column names quoted?
Above, the column names were not quoted, which may seems strange:
you learned that R interprets anything that is not quoted as an object,
and there are no objects called `body_mass` and so on.
But _dplyr_ functions first look for such names among the columns of the data frame,
so _inside these functions_,
you can think of each column as an object (a vector) whose name is the column name.
:::

The **column order** in the output is exactly as you list them in `select()`,
and doesn't need to be the same as in the input data frame.
In other words, `select()` is also one way to reorder columns:
in the example above, we made `body_mass` appear first,
even though it is the sixth column of `penguins`.

You can also specify columns that should be **excluded**,
by prefacing their name with a `!`:

```{r}
select(.data = penguins, !year)
```

### `filter()` to pick rows (observations)

The `filter()` function outputs only those rows that satisfy one or more conditions.

#### Filter based on one condition

This first `filter()` example outputs only rows (penguins) from the island Dream:

```{r}
filter(.data = penguins, island == "Dream")
```

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>How many rows were output?</summary>

124 rows were output, as shown in the first line above: `124 x 8` (rows x columns).

</details>

::: {.callout-warning appearance='simple'}
Remember to use **two** equals signs `==` to test for equality!
:::

#### Filter based on multiple conditions

It's also possible to filter based on multiple conditions.
For example, you may want to see Gentoo penguins with a body mass above 5,000 g:

```{r}
filter(.data = penguins, species == "Gentoo", body_mass > 5000)
```

As in the example above, multiple conditions are by default combined
using a Boolean ***AND***.
In other words, in a given row, _each_ condition must be met to output the row.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Other ways to combine conditions _(Click to expand)_

If you want to combine conditions using a Boolean ***OR***,
where only one of the conditions needs to be met,
use a `|` (vertical bar) between the conditions:

```{r}
# Keep penguins that are either from Dream OR have a body mass above 5,000 g:
filter(.data = penguins, island == "Dream" | body_mass > 5000)
```

To keep rows whose value matches any one of several values,
use the `%in%` operator with a vector of those values ---
for example, to keep penguins from two of the three islands:

```{r}
filter(.data = penguins, island %in% c("Dream", "Biscoe"))
```

:::

### The pipe (`|>`)

Examples so far applied a single _dplyr_ function to a data frame,
simply printing the output (a new data frame) to screen.
But in practice, it's common to use several consecutive _dplyr_ functions to
wrangle a data frame into the format you want.

For example, you may want to first `filter()` rows,
and _then_ `select()` columns.
You could do that as follows:

```{r}
penguins_filt <- filter(.data = penguins, island == "Dream")

select(.data = penguins_filt, species, body_mass)
```

And you could go on like this,
successively creating new objects you use for the next step.
But this should remind you of [the shell pipe](../week04/w4c_shell-files2.qmd#the-pipe):
there, we used `|` to avoid writing intermediate files,
and R has a pipe that avoids creating intermediate objects like `penguins_filt`.

The R **pipe operator** `|>`,
which is a vertical bar <kbd>|</kbd> followed by a greater-than sign <kbd>></kbd>,
directly sends ("pipes") the output of one function into the next function.
Let's start by seeing a rephrasing of the code above, now using pipes:

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(island == "Dream") |>
  select(species, body_mass)
```

What happened here? We took the `penguins` data frame,
sent ("piped") it into the `filter()` function,
whose output in turn was piped into the `select()` function.
You can think of the pipe as **"then"**:
take `penguins`, _then_ filter, _then_ select.

When using the pipe,
you no longer specify the input data frame with the `.data` argument,
because the function now gets its input data via the pipe^[
Specifically, the input goes to the function's first argument by default.] ---
just like `wc` in the shell no longer needed a file name argument
when it got its input via the pipe.

::: {.callout-tip appearance='minimal'}
Using pipes involves less typing and, above all, is more readable than using
successive assignments.

For code readability,
it is good practice to always start a new line after a pipe `|>`,
and to keep the subsequent line(s) _indented_ as Positron will automatically do.
Positron can also [tidy up your code formatting](../bonus/r.qmd#formatting-code-with-air) for you.
:::

::: callout-note
#### Using the pipe keyboard shortcut

In Positron, you can insert a pipe with the keyboard shortcut
<kbd>Ctrl/Cmd</kbd> + <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>M</kbd>.

In code online, you will also often see an older pipe symbol, `%>%`,
which works the same in most cases,
but only when you have one of the tidyverse packages loaded.
:::

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 2: Pipes

1. Use a "pipeline" like above to output a data frame with two
   columns (`island` and `body_mass`) only for Chinstrap penguins.
   How many rows does your output data frame have?

<!----
   <details><summary>Click for the solution</summary>

   ```{r}
   penguins |>
     filter(species == "Chinstrap") |>
     select(island, body_mass)
   ```

   The output data frame has 68 rows and 2 columns.

   </details>
---->

2. The two pipelines below differ only in the order of `filter()` and `select()`.
   **Predict** whether each of them will work, and why. Then run them to check.

   ```r
   penguins |> filter(island == "Dream") |> select(species, body_mass)
   penguins |> select(species, body_mass) |> filter(island == "Dream")
   ```

<!----
   <details><summary>Click for the solution</summary>

   The first works, but the second fails with an error that the `island` column/object can't be found:
   in a pipeline, each function only "sees" the output of the previous step,
   and `select()` already removed the `island` column before `filter()` got the data.

   </details>
---->

:::

### `arrange()` to sort data frames

The `arrange()` function is like sorting functionality in Excel:
it changes the order of rows based on the values in one or more columns^[
Entire rows are always moved together:
it never reorders the values within a single column on its own,
because that would scramble the data.].
Among other things, sorting can help you find observations with the smallest or
largest values for a certain column.

For example, to see the lightest penguins first, sort by `body_mass`:

```{r}
penguins |>
  arrange(body_mass)
```

Default sorting is from small to large for numbers, and alphabetical for character strings.
To sort in reverse order, use the `desc()` (descending) helper function:

```{r}
penguins |>
  arrange(desc(body_mass))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Sorting by multiple columns _(Click to expand)_

To sort by multiple columns,
where ties in the first column are broken by a second column (and so on),
simply list the columns in the appropriate order:

```{r}
# Sort first by species, then from heaviest to lightest within each species:
penguins |>
  arrange(species, desc(body_mass))
```
:::

## Modifying and summarizing data

### `mutate()` to modify columns and create new ones

So far, we've focused on functions that subset and reorganize data frames.
But you haven't yet seen how to make **changes to the values** in the dataframe
or add columns based on **computations** of existing columns.
All of this can be done with the `mutate()` function.

For example, to add a column with the body mass in kilograms:

```{r}
# The syntax is: <new-column> = <operation>
penguins |>
  select(species, body_mass) |>
  mutate(body_mass_kg = body_mass / 1000)
```

Like operations on vectors,
the division was applied to every element of the `body_mass` column.
(We used `select()` first only so that the new column, which is added at the end,
fits on the screen.)

The above example added a new column to the data frame.
To **modify** an existing column rather than adding a new one,
simply "assign back to the same name".
For example, to convert the `body_mass` column itself to kilograms:

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(species, body_mass) |>
  mutate(body_mass = body_mass / 1000)
```

### `summarize()` to compute summary stats

The final _dplyr_ function we'll cover is `summarize()`,
which computes **summaries** of your data **across rows**.
For example, to compute the mean body mass across all penguins:

```{r}
# The syntax is similar to 'mutate': <new-column> = <operation>
penguins |>
  summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass))
```

The result is `NA`, because two penguins have a missing value for `body_mass`.
Just like with vectors, you can get around this with `na.rm = TRUE`:

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarize(mean_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE))
```

The output is still a data frame, but unlike with the previous _dplyr_ functions,
its rows are not the rows of the input:
`summarize()` "**collapses**" the data down, here to a single number.

`summarize()` becomes really powerful in combination with its `.by` argument,
which lets you compute **groupwise** stats.
For example, to get the mean body mass for each species,
along with the number of penguins, using the helper function `n()`, which simply counts rows:

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarize(
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_penguins = n(),
    .by = species
  )
```

`.by` splits a data frame into groups of rows:
here, one group for observations from each species.
The operations in `summarize()` then happen separately for each group,
which is how we ended up with per-species means and counts.

:::exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: `summarize()`

Count the number of penguins for each _combination_ of species and island
(hint: to group by multiple columns, use `.by = c(<column1>, <column2>)`).
Before running your code, **predict** how many rows the output will have.

<details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

The output has 5 rows, not 3 species × 3 islands = 9:
Adelie penguins were found on all three islands,
but Chinstrap penguins only on Dream, and Gentoo penguins only on Biscoe.
`summarize()` only outputs combinations that occur in the data.

```{r}
penguins |>
  summarize(n_penguins = n(), .by = c(species, island))
```

</details>
:::

Counting rows per group is so common that _dplyr_ has a shortcut for it, `count()`,
which does the grouping and counting in one step:

```{r}
penguins |>
  count(species, island)
```

This gives the same counts as the exercise solution,
with the count column named `n`.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### The `group_by()` function _(Click to expand)_

In tutorials and other people's code,
you'll often see groupwise operations written with a separate `group_by()` step
instead of `.by`:

```{r}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(n_penguins = n())
```

Unlike `.by`, `group_by()` creates a grouped data frame,
and that grouping can stick around after `summarize()`.
For example, when you group by two columns,
`summarize()` only removes the _last_ grouping column,
and prints a message that it "has regrouped the output":

```{r}
penguins |>
  group_by(species, island) |>
  summarize(n_penguins = n())
```

The output is still grouped by `species` (see the `# Groups:` line),
which can affect later steps like `mutate()` or `filter()`.
You can remove the grouping by adding `ungroup()` to the pipeline.
With `.by`, the grouping only applies to that single operation,
so you don't have to worry about this.

Another difference is that `group_by()` sorts the output by the grouping columns,
while `.by` keeps the groups in the order they first appear in the data.
:::

## Reading and writing files

So far, you've worked with a data set that comes with R,
but your own data will usually be in files.
As an example, we'll read, modify, and write the metadata of the RNA-seq data set
that you've been working with.

### Reading a TSV file

_readr_  is one of the packages that is loaded as part of the core tidyverse,
and has functions for reading and writing tabular data to and from plain-text
files like CSV (comma-separated) and TSV (tab-separated) files.

The `read_tsv()` function will read TSV files^[
  And `read_csv()` reads CSV files.
] --- for example:

```{r eval= FALSE}
meta <- read_tsv(file = "../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv")
```

```{r echo= FALSE}
meta <- read_tsv(file = "../assets/week13/metadata.tsv")
```

Note that this function is rather chatty,
telling you how many rows and columns it read, and what their data types are.
Let's check the resulting object, which is a tibble:

```{r}
meta
```

### Modifying the metadata

Let's make two changes to the metadata with `mutate()`.
First, we'll shorten the sample IDs
by removing the shared `S` prefix with the `sub()` function,
which does a character-based search-and-replace.
It takes three arguments: the pattern to search for, what to replace the pattern
with, and the subject vector:

```{r}
meta |>
  mutate(
    sample_id = sub(pattern = "S", replacement = "", x = sample_id)
  )
```

#### Setting a custom order with factors

Because character strings are sorted alphabetically,
sorting the metadata table by `time` puts `10dpi` before `24hpi` ---
but 24 hpi is the earlier time point!

To fix this, you can turn the column into a **factor**,
R's way of storing categorical data with a set order of categories ("levels").
(The `species`, `island`, and `sex` columns in `penguins` are already factors.)

```{r}
meta |>
  mutate(time = factor(time, levels = c("24hpi", "10dpi"))) |>
  arrange(time)
```

This order is also respected in plots and statistical analyses,
and you'll use factors like this for the RNA-seq analysis in week 15.

Finally, let's make both changes in a single `mutate()` call,
and assign the result to a new object:

```{r}
meta_clean <- meta |>
  mutate(
    sample_id = sub(pattern = "S", replacement = "", x = sample_id),
    time = factor(time, levels = c("24hpi", "10dpi"))
  )
```

### Writing to files

To write a data frame to a TSV file, you can use the `write_tsv()` function,
with argument `x` for the R object and argument `file` for the file path:

```{r eval=FALSE}
write_tsv(x = meta_clean, file = "metadata_clean.tsv")
```

A plain-text file like this can't store the order of factor levels,
so if you read the file back in, `time` will be a character column again.

If you want to take a look at the file you just created,
find it in the **Explorer** and click on it.
Positron opens CSV and TSV (and even Excel) files in the Data Explorer,
just like a data frame:

<!-- TODO: screenshot of metadata_clean.tsv in the Data Explorer -->

This is a quick way to look at any data file without reading it into R,
for example to check its column names before you read it.
To see the plain text instead,
click the "Open as Plain Text File" button at the top of the Data Explorer.

## Recap and looking forward

- A vector is a collection of elements of a single data type
  (`character`, `double`, `integer`, or `logical`).
  Operations on vectors are vectorized: they happen for each element.
- Comparisons return logicals, and `sum()` on these counts the `TRUE`s.
- Missing values are coded as `NA`;
  use `na.rm = TRUE` to ignore them in functions like `sum()` and `mean()`.
- Each column of a data frame is a vector,
  so different columns can contain different types of data.
- _dplyr_ functions like `select()`, `filter()`, `arrange()`,
  `mutate()`, and `summarize()` manipulate data frames,
  and the pipe `|>` chains them together.
- `read_tsv()` and `write_tsv()` read and write TSV files.
- Factors store categorical data with a set order of categories.

::: callout-note
### Learn more

Two more useful data wrangling skills,
[reshaping with `pivot_wider()` and joining data frames](../bonus/r.qmd#data-wrangling),
are covered on the optional R self-study page.
:::
